analysis.one_liner: Requires health plans to cover addiction treatment with the same cost-sharing as other medical care.
analysis.headline: The bill, with 56 bipartisan cosponsors, never received a committee or floor vote and died when the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required group health plans and individual insurance that cover substance abuse treatment to apply the same deductibles, copays, and day or visit limits to that treatment as they apply to other medical and surgical care. Plans would not have been required to offer addiction treatment at all, and small employers and plans facing cost increases of 1% or more were exempt. The requirements were set to expire in 2005.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, workers and families covered by employer group plans and individual insurance would have gained: plans covering addiction treatment could no longer charge higher deductibles and copays or impose stricter day and visit limits on that treatment than on medical or surgical care. People needing inpatient detox, residential, or outpatient counseling would have had meaningful cost-sharing protection. Members of unions with pre-existing collective bargaining agreements got delayed effective dates under the bill.

how_it_helps.text: Bars group health plans and individual insurers from imposing treatment limits (day or visit caps) or financial requirements (deductibles, coinsurance, cost-sharing, annual or lifetime dollar limits) on substance abuse treatment unless similar limits apply to medical and surgical benefits
Defines covered treatment broadly to include inpatient detoxification, non-hospital residential treatment, outpatient counseling and medication management, and prevention services

Applies the requirement across all three overlapping federal frameworks — the Public Health Service Act, ERISA, and the Internal Revenue Code — so plans could not evade it through one jurisdictional gap
Exempts small employers (2–50 employees) and any plan where the requirement raises costs by 1% or more, limiting the burden on smaller businesses

analysis.who_pays: If passed, employers and health insurers would have borne higher costs when plans could no longer impose tougher deductibles, copays, or visit limits on addiction treatment than on other care; part of that would likely have been passed through to premiums. Small employers (2–50 employees) and any plan facing a cost increase of 1% or more were exempt, concentrating the cost on larger plans.
analysis.who_pays_short: Insurers and large employers, via premiums

drawbacks.text: The bill sunsets on January 1, 2005, so any parity requirement would have been temporary unless Congress reauthorized it
Plans are not required to offer any substance abuse treatment benefit at all; a plan that covers no addiction treatment faces no parity obligation
The 1% increased-cost exemption would let any plan escape the requirement by showing parity costs exceeded that threshold, a broad escape hatch
Covered treatment is limited to abstinence-based services, narrowing the types of medication-based therapy the mandate would protect
The bill expressly allows plans to negotiate lower reimbursement rates with treatment providers, which could limit the real-world value of parity on paper

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and substantial: people fighting addiction would have faced the same deductibles and visit limits as anyone getting surgery or antibiotics, instead of the punitive cost-sharing that kept many out of treatment. The design is weaker than it looks, though: plans could simply decline to cover addiction treatment, the 1% cost exemption is a wide loophole, the abstinence-based definition narrows covered therapies, and the 2005 sunset means the mandate would expire. Still, the main cost — higher premiums spread across insured groups — is modest compared with the barrier the bill would have removed.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees and then to subcommittees, where it sat without a hearing, a vote, or a floor appearance until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 27, 1999 by Rep. Jim Ramstad with 12 original cosponsors from both parties
It was referred to three committees — Commerce, Education and the Workforce, and Ways and Means — and then to three subcommittees
No committee or subcommittee markup, no floor vote, and no Senate companion action appears anywhere in the record; the last recorded activity was a second round of sponsor remarks in March 2000
The 56 cosponsors included 19 Republicans, 36 Democrats, and 1 Independent, yet the bill died in committee

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employers who would have borne higher premiums from parity requirements were better off because the bill died, along with their workers' existing benefit structures. People with untreated addiction, who would have faced equal cost-sharing for treatment, gained nothing from this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and employers who avoided added costs

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan, with 56 cosponsors split 19 Republicans, 36 Democrats, and 1 Independent, but there was no recorded vote because the bill never left committee.

industries.note: The bill would have barred insurers from imposing tougher cost-sharing and visit limits on addiction treatment than on other care, raising covered treatment costs. Insurers' interest in minimizing those obligations runs against patients seeking treatment.

industries.industry: Large employers and employer health plans
industries.note: Large employers and self-insured plans would have absorbed higher premiums when substance abuse benefits had to match medical-surgical cost-sharing. The bill's small-employer and 1%-cost-increase exemptions shielded smaller firms.
Parity requirements would have made covered inpatient, residential, and outpatient addiction services more usable for insured patients, expanding demand for treatment providers.
